newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Samsung keeps Dutch in the dark about Fokker.
newsitem.headline: Samsung keeps Dutch in the dark about Fokker.

text.p: The Dutch government said on Tuesday it had no news of any progress towards a possible takeover of bankrupt plane maker Fokker NV by Samsung Aerospace.
"There's no news. We're still waiting," Economics Ministry spokesman Jan Loman said. "We've done all we can. We're waiting for the Koreans to give us a reaction."
The Dutch government has expressed mounting concern that, eight months after the company was declared bankrupt, there is still no agreement on a plan to relaunch Fokker.

Court-appointed administrators who have been running Fokker since the bankruptcy gave Samsung the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books in September with a view to a possible takeover of its core plane-making business.
An end-of-October deadline came and went, and recent Dutch media reports have said the Seoul government is now reviewing the plans and that a decision could still be several weeks away.
Loman said he did not know the exact role of the South Korean government in assessing a possible bid and Fokker's administrators did not return calls from Reuters.
Samsung views Fokker as a way of breaking into the global aerospace industry but is unwilling to assume all the risks and has sought major investment by the Dutch state.
The Hague has indicated it will provide fresh capital for Fokker and help fund development of a new 125-seat regional jet.
But Samsung is said to have balked at demands for long-term job guarantees in the Netherlands, where labour costs are much higher than in the Far East.

Fokker, founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, is one of the oldest names in the industry and its F27 Friendship turboprop, launched in 1957, was one of the industry's biggest commercial successes.
In more recent years, however, Fokker struggled to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.

In 1993, Daimler Benz Aerospace (DASA) paid 686 million guilders ($409.7 million) for a 51 percent stake in Fokker, but depressed world aircraft markets and a weak dollar saw the company sink into deep losses that had to be met by DASA and the Dutch state.
In January 1996 Daimler cut off all financial support, forcing the company into bankruptcy two months later.
